matches.reason: Both are the depth-unlimited mutual recursion readFieldValue -> readTable/readArray -> readFieldValue (cases 'F' at line 181 and 'A' at line 184), where a few bytes per nesting level buy a stack frame and the consumer's I/O thread dies with a StackOverflowError that bypasses the IOException/MalformedFrameException handling.

Both are readBytes sizing `new byte[(int)contentLength]` from the peer's 4-byte length before readFully, guarded only by `< Integer.MAX_VALUE`, so ~9 wire bytes force a ~2 GiB heap allocation and OutOfMemoryError/GC thrash in the client JVM.

Both are readTable/readArray wrapping the stream in TruncatedInputStream and looping on `available()` with the declared length never checked against the bytes actually remaining, so an over- or under-declared length yields a silently wrong parse (partial/extra entries and a desynchronised remainder of the frame) instead of a rejected frame.

Both are `if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value);` in readTable: a repeated field name is resolved first-wins and the duplicate dropped with no exception or log, so this client can read a different value for a header than the broker/plugin/proxy that routed or authorized on it.

Both are readTable returning Collections.emptyMap() for tableLength == 0 while the normal path returns a HashMap, so a remote peer picks whether the delivered header map is writable and the common read-headers-then-mutate pattern throws UnsupportedOperationException on the empty-table branch.

Both are `new Date(in.readLong()*1000)` in readTimestamp: a peer-controlled 64-bit seconds value multiplied in long arithmetic with no range or overflow check, letting the peer steer the delivered Date to an arbitrary (far past or future) instant that expiry/ordering/replay logic accepts.

Both are readShortstr's `new String(b, "utf-8")` replacing constructor: malformed UTF-8 is accepted and mapped to U+FFFD instead of rejected, so distinct wire byte sequences collapse onto one Java String key (and compose with the first-wins duplicate rule).

Both flag the same set of end-of-life version properties in pom.xml (jetty 9.4, groovy-all 2.4.21 executing at generate-sources, logback 1.2.x, slf4j 1.7.x) as unmaintained branches whose exposure falls on the build/CI host rather than on consumers of the published jar.
